Let

\[
u=(x_3,x_4,\dots,x_{n+1})^T\in \mathbb{R}^{n-1}.
\]

Then the given matrix is block diagonal:

\[
D\alpha^{tr}D\alpha=
\begin{pmatrix}
r^2 & 0\\
0 & I_{n-1}+\dfrac{1}{r^2}uu^T
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Hence

\[
\det(D\alpha^{tr}D\alpha)
=
r^2\det\!\left(I_{n-1}+\frac{1}{r^2}uu^T\right).
\]

The second determinant is a standard rank-one update. By the matrix determinant lemma,

\[
\det(I+Au)=1+\operatorname{tr}(A)
\]

in this case, or equivalently, the eigenvalues of \(I+\frac1{r^2}uu^T\) are

\[
1,\dots,1,\quad 1+\frac{\|u\|^2}{r^2}.
\]

Thus

\[
\det\!\left(I_{n-1}+\frac{1}{r^2}uu^T\right)
=
1+\frac{\|u\|^2}{r^2}
=
1+\frac{x_3^2+\cdots+x_{n+1}^2}{r^2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\det(D\alpha^{tr}D\alpha)
=
r^2\left(1+\frac{x_3^2+\cdots+x_{n+1}^2}{r^2}\right)
=
r^2+x_3^2+\cdots+x_{n+1}^2.
\]

For the parametrization of \(S^n(a)\), the coordinates satisfy

\[
r^2+x_3^2+\cdots+x_{n+1}^2=a^2.
\]

So, on the regular part of the parametrization, i.e. where \(r\neq 0\),

\[
\det(D\alpha^{tr}D\alpha)=a^2.
\]

\[
\boxed{a^2}
\]
